newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian train survivors groggily relive nightmare.
newsitem.headline: Indian train survivors groggily relive nightmare.

text.p: Scores of survivors, rescued from the wreckage of the bombed Indian train, lay huddled in a remote hospital on Tuesday, dazed and bewildered from blasts that killed many of their fellow passengers.
Rescuers had recovered nearly 60 bodies from the train, ripped apart by two bomb blasts in northeastern India on Monday, but officials expected more victims to be found.

"It was 7.15 in the evening. We were travelling easily myself, my brother-in-law and sister. At that time there were three sounds, the first was low and second was loud and the third was very loud," Radheshyam Sharma, travelling from Dibrugarh in Assam to Agra in northern India, told Reuters.
"After that the lights went and the compartment rolled over and over into a paddy field," Sharma said. "My brother-in-law is no more and my sister is in a serious condition."
Sharma was taking his sister to the northern state of Uttar Pradesh for medical treatment.
"It was too dark to see anything but people were calling each other's names for help," he added.

Three of the train's 19 coaches -- each crammed with up to 100 people leaving for the New Year holiday -- were destroyed in the blasts after the train left Kokrajhar station in Assam state for Delhi around 7 p.m. (1330 GMT) on Monday, police said.

About 54 injured passengers have been brought by a relief train to the N.F. Railway hospital -- which is short of basic medical equipment -- at Alipurduar in the neighbouring West Bengal state, hospital officials said.
"It was too dark to see anything. I grabbed my children and waited in the devastated compartment for 35 minutes," said Mahabir Prasad Sarma, manager of a tea estate in Tinsukia in Assam.
"Then people came with torches and we were taken away," said Sarma, who was travelling with his two sons Dilip aged 12 years and Dinesh 10.
Sarma, connected to a saline drip, was lying in a cot in the hospital with injuries to the head and eyes. His two sons were lying on a cot next to him.
"Most of the injuries were head injuries and fractures. All the local people volunteered to help and donated blood," Niyati Roy, a nurse at the hospital, said.
The injured were lying on dirty sheets. Cats roamed the hospital rooms.
"This is a backward place in India. There are no specialist doctors. There is a shortage of equipment, insufficient staff and communications are bad," said Roy.
Down the corridor in the women's ward in the hospital, a woman with her face badly cut and connected to a saline drip, sat up on the hospital bed.
She was travelling with seven members of her family. Two of them, an old man and a child, died in the blast.
Across the ward, another young woman with facial cuts sat up in her bed with one baby behind her and another tucked by her side.
The young woman, who was in a state of severe shock, had lost her elder sister, mother-in-law and father-in-law in the blast.
No group has claimed responsibility for the blast, which authorities blamed on Bodo tribal guerrillas who have waged a violent separatist struggle for nearly a decade.
"Nobody has died since arriving," Roy said. But as the Reuters reporter left the ward one woman, who was gazing distractedly lying prone, lost consciousness.
